procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 20.12.2016 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLA No. 540 of 2000
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi issued a Judgment and Order dated 20.12.2016 in CRLA No. 540 of 2000.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant appealed the High Court's Judgment and Order to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The impugned judgment of the trial Court and the High Court are set aside qua the appellant.
The appellant herein stands acquitted of the offences alleged against him.
If his detention is not required in connection with any other case, he shall be released, forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether a contention regarding non-examination/inadequate examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, causing material prejudice, can be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, even if not argued before the High Court.

facts: The appellant raised an argument before the Supreme Court that their examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) was inadequate and caused them material prejudice.
The Supreme Court determined that this specific argument had not been properly raised or argued before the High Court, and was therefore being raised for the first time at the Supreme Court level.
law: The Court referred to its previous decision in *Shobit Chamar & Anr. v. State of Bihar*.
This precedent established that a plea regarding non-compliance with Section 313 Cr.P.C. could be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court.
The key principle from this precedent is that a trial will not be vitiated by such non-compliance unless the accused can prove that it resulted in material prejudice.
application: Following the precedent set in *Shobit Chamar*, the Supreme Court decided that it could entertain, or "maintain," the appellant's contention at this stage, despite it not being argued previously.

The Court reasoned that it was appropriate to examine the merits of the claim to determine if the alleged failure to properly question the appellant under Section 313 had indeed caused material prejudice or a miscarriage of justice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the contention and decided that an argument regarding prejudicial non-compliance with Section 313 Cr.P.C. can be raised for the first time before it. The Court's decision to hear the argument was based on precedent, with the understanding that the appellant would still have the burden to prove that the procedural lapse actually caused them material prejudice.

issue.issue_text: What is the presumption when a High Court's judgment does not contain a discussion on a particular point allegedly argued before it?

facts: The appellant raised a contention before the Supreme Court regarding non-examination/inadequate examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The appellant alleged that this point was argued before the High Court, but the High Court's judgment did not contain any discussion on it.
In the appeal filed before the Supreme Court, the appellant did not include a specific ground stating that the High Court had failed to consider this particular point despite it being argued.
law: The Supreme Court holds a general presumption that all arguments actually pressed during a hearing in the High Court are noticed and appropriately dealt with in its judgment.
Consequently, if a High Court's judgment does not contain a discussion on a particular point, it is to be assumed prima facie that the point was not argued at the bar.
This presumption can be rebutted, but the burden is on the party making the claim to specifically show that the point was indeed argued but overlooked by the court.
application: The Supreme Court applied this presumption to the case at hand.
It noted that the High Court's judgment was silent on the issue of examination under Section 313.

The Court then looked for evidence to rebut the presumption. It examined the numerous grounds of appeal (A to Z and AA to GG) filed by the appellant and found an "absolute absence" of any contention that the High Court had failed to consider the Section 313 argument despite it being pressed.
This failure to raise such a specific ground in the appeal strengthened the presumption that the point was never argued in the first place.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the High Court's judgment did not discuss the point and the appellant failed to show otherwise (by not even raising it as a ground of appeal), the contention regarding Section 313 was not argued before the High Court. The presumption that a point not discussed was not argued was therefore upheld.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-compliance with the mandate for questioning under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, caused material prejudice or miscarriage of justice to the appellant.

facts: The appellant was convicted for murder under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Penal Code, 1860.
The conviction for murder was based on a finding of 'common intention'.

This finding of common intention was derived from two key incriminating circumstances appearing in the prosecution's evidence: (1) the appellant's exhortation to kill the deceased and his family, and (2) the appellant allegedly holding the deceased's hands to allow a co-accused to stab him.
During his mandatory examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), the appellant was not questioned about either of these two specific incriminating circumstances.
law: Section 313(1)(b) of the Cr.P.C. makes it mandatory for the court to question an accused person on any incriminating circumstances that have appeared in the evidence against them.

The purpose of this questioning is to provide the accused an opportunity to personally explain these circumstances, in line with the principles of natural justice ('audi alteram partem' - hear the other side).
Mere non-compliance or inadequate questioning under Section 313 does not automatically vitiate a trial.
To vitiate the trial, the convict bears the onus of establishing that the non-compliance resulted in 'material prejudice' or a 'miscarriage of justice'.
application: The Supreme Court examined the record of the appellant's questioning under Section 313 and confirmed that the two crucial incriminating circumstances—the exhortation and the act of holding the victim—were not put to him.
The Court noted that the trial court's entire conclusion that the appellant shared a 'common intention' to commit murder was based solely on these two pieces of evidence.

By failing to question the appellant on these specific points, the trial court deprived him of his mandatory right and opportunity to explain the very evidence that formed the foundation of his conviction.

The Court reasoned that this was not a minor procedural lapse but a fundamental defect. Since the conviction for common intention rested exclusively on the circumstances he was never asked to explain, the failure to question him directly caused material prejudice.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the non-compliance with the mandatory requirement of Section 313 of the Cr.P.C. caused material prejudice to the appellant. Because the conviction was based entirely on two incriminating circumstances that he was never given an opportunity to explain, the trial was vitiated. Therefore, the Court accepted the appellant's argument.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a contention regarding non-examination/inadequate examination under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, causing material prejudice, can be raised for the first time before the Supreme Court, even if not argued before the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The appellant raised the contention that the non-examination under Section 313 Cr.PC caused material prejudice, implying that such a fundamental flaw should be considered by the Supreme Court regardless of whether it was argued before the High Court.
respondent_arguments: The text does not indicate that the respondent objected to this contention being raised for the first time. Instead, the respondent's counsel conceded on the merits of the Section 313 issue.

arguments.issue_text: What is the presumption when a High Court's judgment does not contain a discussion on a particular point allegedly argued before it?
appellant_arguments: The appellant did not specifically challenge the presumption but proceeded to argue the point on Section 313, implying it should be considered an exception. The appellant also did not include any ground in the appeal stating that the High Court had failed to consider an argument that was actually pressed before it.
respondent_arguments: The text does not contain a specific argument from the respondent on this point, but typically the respondent would rely on such a presumption to argue that the point was never raised and should therefore be considered waived.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the non-compliance with the mandate for questioning under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, caused material prejudice or miscarriage of justice to the appellant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant contended that incriminating circumstances that appeared in the prosecution evidence were not put to them during the Section 313 examination, and this failure resulted in material prejudice and a miscarriage of justice.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's counsel fairly admitted that the material on record revealed the correctness of the appellant's contentions on this issue.

statutes.act_name: Code of Criminal Procedure (Amendment) Act, 2008 (Act 5 of 2009)

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is the duty of the Trial Court to put each material circumstance appearing in the evidence against the accused specifically, distinctively and separately. The material circumstance means the circumstance or the material on the basis of which the prosecution is seeking his conviction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In cases involving serious offences with extreme penalties, a failure to comply with the mandatory procedural safeguard of questioning the accused on all incriminating circumstances under Section 313 Cr.PC can vitiate the trial. The Supreme Court, as a court for the dispensation of justice, is bound to consider whether such a failure caused material prejudice or a miscarriage of justice, even if the issue was not raised in the lower courts, to correct the mistake and prevent an unjust outcome.
legal_tests_applied: The court must determine if non-compliance with Section 313 Cr.PC caused "material prejudice or miscarriage of justice" to the accused.

The maxim “actus curiae neminem gravabit” – “the act of court shall prejudice no one” – requires the court to correct its own mistakes rather than directing the affected party to seek a remedy elsewhere.
The court must ordinarily eschew material circumstances not put to the accused from consideration while dealing with the case of that particular accused.
When deciding if prejudice was caused by an omission in the Section 313 examination, the delay in raising the contention is only one of several factors to be considered.
policy_considerations: In a charge for commission of a serious offence where extreme penalty alone is imposable in case the accused is found guilty, procedural safeguards ensuring protection of right(s) of accused must be followed.

When non-compliance of a mandatory procedure capable of vitiating a trial is raised and revealed from the records, it must be considered irrespective of whether it was raised appropriately before, lest the consideration of the case result in a miscarriage of justice.

Being the Court existing for dispensation of justice, this Court is bound to consider and correct the mistake committed by the Court by looking into the question whether non-examination or inadequate examination of accused concerned caused material prejudice or miscarriage of justice.
